title: A giving review
hook: once a year, look at what you gave
tomorrow: why is it easier to be kind to strangers than at home?

segments.voice: Yesterday, water and a name, given before anything was earned: remember whose you are. Today, a look back at what went out of your hands.
screen: `REMEMBER WHOSE YOU ARE.` → `WHAT WENT OUT OF YOUR HANDS?`

segments.voice: At the end of the year, the apps hand you a recap: your top songs, your steps, the places you went. Nobody sends a giving recap. If one existed, it would show more than money: the hours, the rides, the meal dropped off, the few dollars for a friend's fundraiser. And it would show whether any of it was planned, or only leftover. Jesus once sat and watched people give, and he did the math differently.
screen: `A RECAP OF EVERYTHING.` → `NOBODY SENDS A GIVING RECAP.` → `JESUS DID THE MATH DIFFERENTLY.`

segments.voice: At the Temple treasury, rich people put in large gifts. Then a poor widow drops in two small coins. Jesus calls his friends over: “this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury.” They gave out of plenty, he says; she “of her want did cast in all that she had.” Here's the one to tell a friend tonight: the smallest gift in the story is the one Jesus points out. He measured the cost to the giver, not the size. In Luke he gives a rule of thumb: “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much.” Small, steady faithfulness is where the larger kind grows. Paul adds the spirit of it: “Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” Purposeth in his heart: giving here is decided, not just something that happens. He even suggests setting it aside “upon the first day of the week.” That's what a giving review is for. Once a year, look back at what you gave: money, time, skill, attention. Was it planned or leftover? Cheerful or grudging? Christians answer how much in different ways; some aim for a tithe, some give as they're able, some give mostly time. The review isn't a scorecard. It's the heart deciding again.
screen: `TWO SMALL COINS, AND MORE.` · `FAITHFUL IN THE LEAST.` · `PURPOSETH IN HIS HEART.` · `PLANNED, OR LEFTOVER?` · then, large: `FAITHFUL IN MUCH.`

segments.voice: Count on your fingers what you gave this past year, and not only money: an afternoon, a ride, a listening ear, a skill. When your fingers run out, pick one you'd like to give again on purpose. Hold that one through the rest of the sit.
A giving review. Once a year, a look back at what you gave, money, time and attention, and a chance to decide again.
Your line: faithful in much. It grows out of small, steady giving that someone chose. That's day seventeen-thirteen.

screen: `DAY 1713 COUNTS.` → `LIVING IT · 32 OF 70.` → `TOMORROW: WHY IS KINDNESS HARDER AT HOME?`

howItsDone: Some Christians set a yearly time to look back at their giving of money, time and skill and adjust it; some aim for a tithe, a tenth, while others give as they're able or give mostly time.

chat.says: did my giving math. it's SO small. should i just put all my savings in the plate sunday?
options: Start small and steady. Faithful in least, faithful in much. Plan an amount you can keep.
Yes. The widow gave everything she had, so all of it is the only real gift.
Wait until you earn more. Small amounts don't really count for much anyway.
chat.meaning: Luke 16:10: faithful in the least is faithful in much. Paul: give as you've decided in your heart, cheerfully, not grudgingly or under pressure.
